extracted.intended_audience: general readers, journalists, students and researchers interested in free expression, satire, and the Jyllands-Posten controversy
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards relevant to creating, publishing, or republishing political/satirical cartoons that depict religious figures, and how legal, journalistic, diplomatic and safety considerations bear on those decisions. Focus is on the Danish/European context but includes general principles about public interest and respect for rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 140 (blasphemy law) / prohibition on ridiculing religious dogmas
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 140 (aka the blasphemy law) prohibited disturbing public order by publicly ridiculing or insulting the dogmas of worship of any lawfully existing religious community in Denmark.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historically rarely used (last sentence 1938, no conviction since 1938 cited). A complaint under this section was filed against Jyllands-Posten but the prosecutor declined to file charges; the statute was repealed in 2017. Use of this standard assesses whether publication 'disturbs public order' by ridiculing religious dogma.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 266b (criminalisation of hate/insult against protected groups)
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 266b criminalises insult, threat or degradation of natural persons by publicly and with malice attacking their race, colour of skin, national or ethnic roots, faith or sexual orientation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provision was invoked in complaints about the cartoons. Legal evaluation under 266b examines whether an expression is a malicious public attack on a protected group's dignity rather than legitimate public-interest satire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of freedom of expression in Denmark (public interest / editorial freedom)
rubrics_metrics.description: The freedom of expression in Denmark has a wide scope; Danish legislation prohibits certain acts (libel, hate speech, blasphemy) but editorial freedom is extended regarding subjects of public interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Regional Public Prosecutor discontinued the investigation into the cartoons because the publication concerned a subject of public interest and Danish case law extends editorial freedom for such subjects. In assessing offences, the right to freedom of speech must be weighed against other human rights (protection against discrimination, insult and degradation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Balancing free speech with respect for other human rights
rubrics_metrics.description: Freedom of speech must be exercised with the necessary respect for other human rights, including the right to protection against discrimination, insult and degradation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prosecutors and courts consider both the public-interest value of speech and its potential to infringe other rights; this balancing informs decisions on prosecution or permissible publication. Authorities noted there is 'no free and unrestricted right' to express opinions about religious subjects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public interest / newsworthiness as a defence for controversial publication
rubrics_metrics.description: Publication of material on matters of public interest may justify editorial freedom even if the material offends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The prosecutor's discontinuation of the criminal investigation cited that the cartoons concerned a public-interest subject. Editors and courts may weigh newsworthiness, debate value and context when determining acceptability or legal liability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journalistic validity / sound editorial basis for publishing (methodological rigor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalistic decisions should be based on valid methods and sound editorial reasoning; experiments or surveys lacking validity undermine the journalistic basis for publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics argued the Jyllands-Posten 'experiment' lacked validity and that the story 'fell short of sound journalistic basis.' Editors chose to publish the cartoons as an opinion/culture piece rather than as news due to inconclusive results. This criterion covers whether the editorial framing and evidence justify publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-censorship and evidence of intimidation as justification for publication
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims of self-censorship (artists refusing work out of fear) can be used to justify investigative or critical publications exploring threats to free expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The initiative was presented as testing the degree to which illustrators felt threatened; evidence of refusals due to fear influenced the editorial decision. Assessments should verify claims (e.g., confirm artists' statements) because unverified claims weaken the justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy and reliability of advocacy/complaint materials (e.g., dossiers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Materials used to mobilise outrage or diplomatic action must be accurate and not include false or misattributed images or claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Akkari-Laban dossier included several images and assertions some of which were false or misleading (e.g., a pig-squealing contest photo misrepresented as a cartoon). Experts said such mistakes could mislead audiences unfamiliar with the context and polarise the situation. Advocacy materials should avoid unverified additions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intent and context (satire vs gratuitous offence / incitement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluation considers whether drawings are satirical, intended as criticism/comment about religion or society, or are gratuitously offensive or inciting hatred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supporters argued the cartoons were legitimate free-speech satire treating Islam as other religions are treated; opponents saw them as insulting the faith. Courts and commentators weigh intent and context in distinguishing protected satire from unlawful incitement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Safety and security risks as an editorial consideration
rubrics_metrics.description: Potential threats to staff, property, and public safety must be considered when deciding to publish or reprint provocative imagery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After threats, cartoonists went into hiding and some publications chose not to reprint material citing security concerns (e.g., Jyllands-Posten did not re-print Charlie Hebdo cartoons after attacks). Editors may weigh the value of publication against likely security costs and risks to personnel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diplomatic and international-relation consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Publication that offends foreign communities can provoke diplomatic protests, boycotts, attacks on embassies and affect bilateral relations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ambassadors and governments sought meetings and protested; some countries organised boycotts and attacks on diplomatic missions occurred. Decision-makers may consider potential international fallout when publishing inflammatory material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal recourse and procedural route for offended parties
rubrics_metrics.description: Offended parties may bring acts or expressions to court; it is for the courts to decide in individual cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Danish government stated it could not influence the press and that offended parties have legal avenues. Understanding procedural possibilities and past case law informs both publishers and complainants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial remedies and public responses (apology vs defence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishers may respond to controversy with apologies, clarifications or a defence of publication and freedom of expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jyllands-Posten published open letters apologising for any offence while defending the right to publish. Choosing how to respond publicly is a normative editorial criterion balancing accountability, apology, and defence of principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of reprinting policies across media and jurisdictions
rubrics_metrics.description: Different outlets and countries may choose to reprint or not based on legal environment, cultural sensitivity, security, and editorial stance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The cartoons were reprinted in some European newspapers but declined by many North American outlets, reflecting factors including legal risk, cultural sensitivity and wartime context. Reprinting decisions should account for varied local laws and audience composition.
